chapters.name: Intro
sentences: For twenty-seven years, you could fly from London to New York faster than the sun crosses the sky.
You took off after breakfast, and landed, by the local clock, before you had left.
The plane was Concorde. It was beautiful, it was fast, and nothing like it has carried passengers since.
So why did the most famous airliner in history fail?
In this video, we follow Concorde from a bold idea in the nineteen sixties, to its very last flight.
The answer is not one thing. It is a chain of costs, rules, noise, and in the end, a tragedy.

chapters.name: Two Countries, One Dream
sentences: In the nineteen sixties, the future of flying looked supersonic. Faster than the speed of sound.
Britain and France both wanted to build a supersonic airliner. But neither country could afford to do it alone.
So they joined forces. British and French engineers would design one aircraft together.
Even its name was a symbol. Concorde means agreement, or harmony.
The plan was simple. Build the fastest passenger jet in the world, and sell it to airlines everywhere.
Concorde first flew in nineteen sixty-nine. For a while, it looked like the dream was coming true.

chapters.name: The Cost Explodes
sentences: But building something that had never existed was far harder than anyone had planned.
Concorde had to cruise at twice the speed of sound for hours. At that speed, air friction heats the skin of the aircraft.
In fact, the heat made the whole aircraft stretch. In flight, Concorde grew slightly longer, and engineers had to design for that too.
Its engines, its wings, and even its drooping nose had to be invented, tested, and invented again.
Each delay cost money. And each problem led to another delay.
The first estimate for the project was about seventy million pounds.
In the end, the cost rose to more than one point three billion pounds. Some estimates go even higher.
That money came mostly from taxpayers in Britain and France.

chapters.name: The Orders Vanish
sentences: At first, airlines were excited. Sixteen airlines placed orders, for more than seventy aircraft.
Then the world changed.
In nineteen seventy-three, an oil crisis made jet fuel far more expensive. A thirsty supersonic jet suddenly looked like a terrible business.
At the same time, a very different aircraft was arriving. The Boeing seven forty-seven. It was slower, but it could carry far more people, much more cheaply.
One by one, the orders were cancelled. One expert later said they started to drop like a run on a bank.
Without enough buyers, there was no way to earn back the enormous amount of money spent on development.
In the end, only two airlines flew Concorde: British Airways and Air France. Each operated seven aircraft.
Only twenty Concordes were ever built, including six that were used for development and testing.

chapters.name: The Boom Problem
sentences: There was another problem, and you could hear it.
When an aircraft flies faster than sound, it creates a shock wave. On the ground, people hear a loud double bang, called a sonic boom.
Concorde's boom trailed behind it in a path about sixteen miles wide.
In nineteen seventy-three, the United States banned supersonic flight over land. So Concorde could only fly at full speed over the ocean.
Over land, Concorde had to fly slower than sound, just like any other jet. Its one great advantage disappeared.
Noise at airports was a problem too. Complaints delayed its service to New York until nineteen seventy-seven.
And its range was only about four thousand five hundred miles. That was enough to cross the Atlantic, but not the Pacific.
So the routes where speed would have mattered most, like Europe to Asia, were simply out of reach.

chapters.name: Flying at Mach 2
sentences: Still, for those who flew it, Concorde was unforgettable.
Passenger service began in January, nineteen seventy-six.
It cruised at about twice the speed of sound, as high as sixty thousand feet. From the window, the sky looked dark, and the earth's curve was visible.
For takeoff and landing, its long pointed nose drooped down, so the pilots could see the runway in front of them.
London to New York took about three and a half hours. That is less than half the time of a normal jet.
But there were only about one hundred seats, in a narrow cabin.
And a round-trip ticket could cost around ten thousand dollars. Concorde became a symbol of luxury, for celebrities and business leaders.

chapters.name: The Numbers Never Worked
sentences: Behind the glamour, the numbers were hard to ignore.
Concorde burned about six thousand seven hundred gallons of fuel per hour. A Boeing seven forty-seven burned about three thousand six hundred.
But the seven forty-seven carried several times as many passengers.
Per passenger, Concorde travelled about sixteen miles for each gallon. The seven forty-seven managed about forty-six.
One estimate says Concorde burned around two thousand pounds of fuel for every passenger crossing the Atlantic.
Maintenance was enormous too. Concorde needed about eighteen hours of work for every hour in the air.
And as the fleet grew older, spare parts and repairs became even more expensive.
By the end, New York was the only regular destination left. The other routes had been losing money.

chapters.name: July 2000
sentences: On the twenty-fifth of July, two thousand, a Concorde took off from Paris, heading for New York.
During the takeoff run, it ran over a strip of metal that had fallen from another airliner.
A tyre burst. Pieces struck the wing, a fuel tank ruptured, and a fire started.
Minutes later, the plane crashed near Paris. One hundred and thirteen people died, including people on the ground.
It was the only fatal accident in Concorde's history.
The whole fleet was grounded for more than a year, while engineers made changes costing about seventeen million pounds.
The changes included new protection inside the fuel tanks, and stronger tyres.

chapters.name: The Last Flight
sentences: Concorde returned to service in late two thousand and one. But the timing could not have been worse.
After the attacks of September the eleventh, air travel fell sharply. Many of Concorde's best customers stopped flying.
Seats were empty. Costs kept rising.
And the aircraft themselves were getting old. Keeping them flying safely was becoming harder every year.
In two thousand three, British Airways and Air France announced that Concorde would retire.
The last commercial flight landed on the twenty-fourth of October, two thousand three.
Crowds gathered to watch. For many people, it felt like the end of the future.

chapters.name: What Concorde Teaches
sentences: So, did Concorde fail?
As a piece of engineering, it was a triumph. It flew passengers at twice the speed of sound for almost three decades.
As a business, it struggled from the start. One aviation expert summed it up simply.
Concorde, he said, was more about technological prowess than economical reality.
The lesson is one that every aircraft maker now remembers. A plane is not only a machine. It must also make sense for the airlines that buy it, and for the people who live beneath its path.
Today, engineers are still working on quieter supersonic designs, and they study Concorde's story closely.
Speed alone was not enough.

chapters.name: Outro
sentences: Today, you can still see Concorde in museums in Britain, France and the United States.
Standing next to it, it still looks like the future.
